joshua.title: Joshua AI Agent
joshua.subtitle: AI Copywriting Agent powered by KoGPT-2

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.background: Joshua AI Agent is an AI-powered copywriting service built on the KoGPT-2 language model. It's a subscription-based desktop application that generates marketing content and advertising copy, supporting both Windows and macOS through a cross-platform architecture. The project required integrating a FastAPI backend with PostgreSQL database for AI model serving, where I was responsible for the frontend development. The key technical challenges included integrating Angular framework within Electron environment, implementing real-time streaming rendering of AI responses, and adapting the Stripe payment flow for desktop application context.
overview.contribution: I led all aspects of frontend development, from designing the Electron + Angular desktop application architecture to implementing the AI response interface and Stripe payment integration. I designed the IPC (Inter-Process Communication) structure between Electron's Main and Renderer processes, handling backend API communication in the Main process while keeping the Angular-based Renderer process focused purely on UI rendering and user interaction. For progressive streaming display of AI-generated content, I built an asynchronous data processing pipeline using RxJS. I also customized Stripe's Checkout session-based payment flow to fit the desktop environment.

retrospective.title: Retrospective
retrospective.growth: Developing a cross-platform desktop application combining Electron and Angular deepened my understanding of architecture for building native apps with web technology stacks. I learned a great deal solving unique problems that arise when combining web frameworks with desktop environments, including IPC communication structure design, Main/Renderer process role separation, and Angular Zone.js interaction with Electron's event loop. Experience with RxJS-based asynchronous data streaming proved valuable in subsequent projects. Stripe payment integration gave me capabilities for implementing SaaS business model frontends. Implementing an interface that renders AI model responses in real-time streaming made me realize the importance of UX design that transforms 'waiting' into 'experiencing' beyond simply displaying data.
retrospective.improvement: Early in the project, I struggled with limited references for Electron-Angular integration through much trial and error. More thorough technical validation (POC) upfront would have accelerated development. Insufficient test code for the IPC communication layer consumed considerable debugging time—systematic unit and integration tests for Main-Renderer communication logic would have improved stability. From a performance optimization perspective, more thorough bundle size optimization (tree-shaking, lazy loading) and memory profiling could have improved app launch speed and resource usage. In future similar projects, I plan to clearly establish testing strategy and performance goals during initial design, with continuous monitoring and improvement.

challenge1.title: Electron IPC Architecture Design
challenge1.context: In Electron's separated Main↔Renderer process model, I needed to safely synchronize AI inference requests, Stripe payment events, and UI state. Unlike a browser app where a simple fetch suffices, IPC channel design in a desktop app directly determines overall application stability.
challenge1.alternatives: Making external API calls directly from the Renderer was rejected due to security vulnerabilities (API key exposure) and CORS issues. A single-process Node.js CLI app was rejected because it couldn't incorporate the UI/UX designed with the team's designers and failed to meet the SI delivery requirement for a GUI application.
challenge1.decision: I chose Electron + Angular, with a strict IPC separation where the Main process handles all external communication (FastAPI, Stripe) while the Renderer focuses purely on UI. Angular's DI system and RxJS streaming were well-suited for real-time AI response rendering, and the client required cross-platform support for both Windows and macOS.
challenge1.implementation: The ipcMain relays inference requests to the FastAPI server, and the ipcRenderer subscribes to AI responses as an RxJS Observable stream. Stripe webhook events are also processed in the Main process, propagating payment status changes (feature lock/unlock) to the UI.
challenge1.outcome: Successfully delivered the SI project on schedule and launched a Windows/macOS cross-platform desktop application. The full development cycle was completed by a 3-person team (2 designers, 1 planning & development).

challenge2.title: KoGPT-2 Inference Pipeline Optimization
challenge2.context: I fine-tuned KoGPT-2 to auto-generate Korean copywriting text, but the default generation settings produced excessive unnecessary tokens, causing response latency and quality degradation. Fast response was a critical requirement for the SI delivery environment.
challenge2.alternatives: Using GPT-3/ChatGPT API was rejected because Korean copywriting quality was unstable in 2022, reliance on an external API made offline support impossible, and the cost structure was incompatible with the SI delivery model. Rule-based template generation was rejected for lacking keyword combination diversity and being unable to produce the creative copy marketers expected.
challenge2.decision: I chose KoGPT-2 fine-tuning on a self-configured GPU bare-metal server. I designed a keyword-centric prompt structure and applied generation parameter tuning to reduce unnecessary token output. The internal GPU server was used like an inference-serving platform to handle requests reliably.
challenge2.implementation: I structured prompts around input keywords so the model focused on relevant context. Generation parameters such as top-k and temperature were experimentally adjusted to balance output quality and speed. A FastAPI server exposed the inference endpoint, which the Electron Main process called via IPC.
challenge2.outcome: Tuning top-k and temperature parameters reduced unnecessary token generation and achieved a response speed suitable for real-time production use. A 3-person team delivered the SI project on schedule and shipped the app simultaneously on 2 platforms (Windows and macOS).

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.background: DY Microfinance ERP is a web-based management system designed to automate customer management and accounting operations for a Myanmar-based microfinance institution. Previously, customer information, loan records, and accounting ledgers were managed manually using Excel spreadsheets, leading to frequent data integrity issues and requiring dozens of hours of manual work during month-end closing. To address this, I adopted a separated architecture connecting a Next.js frontend with a NestJS backend via PostgreSQL database. As a solo developer handling both frontend and backend, I focused on admin dashboard UI/UX design and implementation, complex accounting data table management, and form validation logic on the frontend side.
overview.contribution: I was responsible for the entire process from system architecture design to deployment. From a frontend perspective, I implemented an admin dashboard based on Next.js App Router, form processing using Server Actions, accounting data table rendering optimization, and bilingual support (Burmese/English). The dashboard visualizes key metrics like customer count, loan balance, and monthly revenue in real-time, enabling management to grasp the current situation at a glance. Through accounting process automation, I built an interface that auto-generates BS (Balance Sheet) and PL (Profit & Loss) statements, eliminating approximately 90% of manual work and reducing month-end closing time from dozens of hours to just a few hours. I also implemented Role-Based Access Control at the frontend routing level, ensuring users (loan officers, accounting staff, administrators) can only access screens and features relevant to their roles.

retrospective.title: Retrospective
retrospective.growth: As a solo full-stack developer designing and implementing both frontend and backend, I deepened my understanding of overall web application architecture. Particularly using Next.js App Router, Server Components, and Server Actions in production helped me experience the pros and cons of SSR and CSR firsthand, enabling me to judge which rendering strategy to choose in different situations. Configuring a separated frontend-backend architecture built practical skills essential for real-world work: API design, ensuring type safety, and handling authentication/authorization. Implementing dashboard and data visualization UI improved my UX design ability to translate complex business logic into user-friendly interfaces. Through accounting process automation, I experienced the value of development that creates 'business impact' beyond mere 'feature implementation,' finding great satisfaction in continuously improving based on user feedback.
retrospective.improvement: Delaying test code writing early in the project led to occasional regression issues where new features broke existing ones. Especially for critical accuracy areas like accounting logic, unit and integration tests are essential—skipping them due to schedule pressure was regrettable. In the future, I want to adopt TDD (Test-Driven Development) or at least ensure test coverage for core business logic. CI/CD pipeline setup was also insufficient. Manual SSH deployment to servers could have been faster and more stable with automated deployment pipelines using GitHub Actions. For performance monitoring, introducing tools like Sentry or LogRocket to track production errors and performance bottlenecks in real-time would have enabled faster problem resolution. In my next project, I plan to establish testing, CI/CD, and monitoring from the start to build more stable and maintainable systems.

challenge1.title: Frontend-Backend Separated Architecture Design
challenge1.context: DY Microfinance's existing workflow relied on Excel spreadsheets and manual processes, requiring dozens of hours for month-end closing and causing frequent data integrity errors. I needed to migrate to a systematic digital system while maintaining maintainability and scalability as a solo full-stack developer.
challenge1.alternatives: A monolithic full-stack framework (e.g., Django) was rejected because it offered lower frontend flexibility and made implementing a modern SPA-style admin dashboard difficult. Firebase/Supabase BaaS was rejected because the complex accounting calculation logic unique to microfinance is hard to implement serverlessly, and real-time DB dependency was unsuitable for Myanmar's local network conditions.
challenge1.decision: I selected a separated architecture: Next.js App Router (frontend) + NestJS (backend) + PostgreSQL. Server Actions simplified form handling, and NestJS's module system allowed accounting logic to be organized by domain. Even as a solo developer, establishing a clear frontend/backend boundary enabled a structure ready for team division if the system later expanded into an ERP.
challenge1.implementation: I implemented loan/repayment transaction CRUD and automatic BS/PL calculation APIs in NestJS, and applied RBAC-based routing (3 roles: loan officer, accountant, admin) in the Next.js dashboard. Server Actions validated form submissions server-side before calling NestJS APIs.
challenge1.outcome: Achieved approximately 90% automation of the overall accounting process. Reduced month-end closing time from dozens of hours to just a few hours. The system stability was sufficient to prompt ongoing discussions about ERP expansion.

challenge2.title: RBAC Role-Based Access Control Implementation
challenge2.context: In microfinance operations, loan officers, accountants, and administrators have clearly distinct responsibilities. If a loan officer could modify accounting data or a non-admin could change system settings, financial data integrity would be at risk. Role-based access control was a core business requirement.
challenge2.alternatives: Applying only simple page-level route guards was rejected because guarding only the frontend without API-level validation allows bypassing via direct API calls. External auth services (Auth0, Clerk) were rejected due to the need to minimize external service dependency in Myanmar's local internet environment, and the cost structure was excessive for a small user base of dozens of accounts.
challenge2.decision: I implemented a self-built JWT-based RBAC system. NestJS Guards handle role validation, and Next.js middleware provides route-level access control — creating a dual-layer enforcement. I defined the role-based permission matrix directly, drawing on real microfinance accounting and operations experience.
challenge2.implementation: NestJS includes a role claim in JWT tokens, and custom Guard decorators enforce role validation per API endpoint. The Next.js frontend filters route access via middleware and renders different dashboard layouts based on role. Separate menus and data access scopes were defined for each of the 3 roles (loan officer / accountant / admin).
challenge2.outcome: Enforced role-based access control at both frontend routing and backend API layers, securing data integrity and protecting financial records previously managed manually and in scattered spreadsheets. Established a safe multi-user environment underpinning ~90% accounting automation.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.background: A system deployed in retail stores in Malaysia that uses YOLO object detection models to track customer movement in real-time. It recognizes customer positions and movement paths from CCTV footage, collecting data on how long customers stay at which displays and what routes they take through the store. This enables store managers to understand customer behavior patterns and gain insights for optimizing display positioning and improving traffic flow. On the backend, a PyTorch-implemented YOLO model performs real-time video processing, while the frontend receives this data and visualizes it in dashboard form. For the frontend tech stack, VanillaJS (pure JavaScript) was deliberately chosen to validate whether complex real-time data visualization could be implemented without frameworks like React or Vue, and to optimize bundle size and performance.
overview.contribution: I was responsible for all frontend data visualization aspects, building a real-time dashboard with VanillaJS. I implemented heatmap and movement tracking visualizations using Canvas API and SVG, receiving customer location data transmitted via WebSocket from the backend team. I displayed customers' current positions in real-time on the store floor plan, created heatmaps using color gradients to show customer density by time period, and connected individual customer movement paths with lines for tracking. I also implemented statistical charts (visitor count by time, dwell time by zone, etc.) using the Chart.js library. Since I had to perform state management and DOM manipulation without a framework, I designed simple state management patterns (Observer pattern) and component separation structure myself. I applied rendering optimizations (RequestAnimationFrame, Debouncing) to efficiently process incoming real-time data and implemented event listener cleanup logic to prevent memory leaks.

retrospective.title: Retrospective
retrospective.growth: Implementing a complex real-time dashboard without frameworks using VanillaJS deepened my understanding of JavaScript's fundamental operation principles and browser rendering mechanisms. Directly handling Canvas API and SVG built low-level graphics rendering experience, strengthening crucial real-world frontend development capabilities like real-time data processing via WebSocket, memory management, and performance optimization. Particularly designing and implementing state management patterns myself helped me understand how state management libraries provided by React or Vue work internally, enabling deeper utilization when later using Redux or Vuex. Solving memory leak and rendering performance issues taught me profiling techniques using Chrome DevTools, and I gained valuable experience applying optimization patterns frequently used in practice like requestAnimationFrame, Debouncing, and Observer pattern. Through Canvas-based data visualization, I learned efficient methods for representing large datasets, which greatly helped when implementing charts or graphs in subsequent projects.
retrospective.improvement: Developing with VanillaJS made me acutely feel the necessity of frameworks. Without convenience features modern frameworks provide—component reusability, declarative UI, virtual DOM—implementing everything manually was slow and created much code duplication. Particularly manually managing data synchronization across modules and DOM update logic was cumbersome and frequently caused bugs from mistakes. Had I used React, state management could have been simply handled with useState or useReducer, and Canvas rendering managed with useEffect for much more concise code. Also, component-based structure could have separated charts, heatmaps, and movements into independent components for improved reusability and testability. In the project's latter half, I thought 'React would have been right for this scale.' I realized VanillaJS is suitable for small-scale interactive elements or legacy system maintenance, but has limits for building complex SPAs. In future similar projects, I learned the importance of considering project scale and complexity when choosing technology to select appropriate frameworks. Next time, I want to build a better structured data visualization dashboard using a React + D3.js combination.

challenge1.title: VanillaJS Real-Time Data Visualization Architecture
challenge1.context: I needed to visualize customer movement paths, dwell time, and congestion data extracted by YOLO from store CCTV footage in real-time on a dashboard. Data refreshed every second, and the rendering pipeline had to simultaneously handle Canvas/SVG heatmaps and WebSocket streaming under high-performance requirements.
challenge1.alternatives: React was rejected because virtual DOM diffing overhead causes unnecessary re-renders during second-level real-time Canvas updates, and the framework abstraction interferes with directly drawing YOLO analysis results to Canvas. Bundle size also grows unnecessarily in an on-premise environment. Using D3.js alone was rejected because while it excels at heatmap visualization, handling WebSocket real-time data ingestion and state management through D3 alone would sharply increase code complexity.
challenge1.decision: I chose VanillaJS to implement visualization directly with Canvas API and SVG heatmaps, using the Observer pattern for state management and WebSocket for real-time data ingestion. Rendering was optimized with requestAnimationFrame and debouncing, and external dependencies were minimized to ensure stable operation on the on-premise store server environment.
challenge1.implementation: A WebSocket connection received real-time customer coordinate and behavior data from the YOLO analysis server. The Observer pattern propagated data changes to subscribing view components. Customer movement paths were drawn to Canvas, and dwell time was color-mapped to an SVG heatmap. requestAnimationFrame targeted 60fps rendering, while debouncing throttled excessive WebSocket event processing.
challenge1.outcome: Implemented a real-time dashboard visualizing 3 key behavioral metrics — customer movement paths, dwell time, and congestion — providing stakeholders with a data-driven environment to optimize store layout and product placement strategy.

challenge2.title: YOLO-Based On-Premise Video Analysis Pipeline
challenge2.context: I needed to identify and track customers in existing CCTV footage from Malaysian retail stores to extract behavioral data. The store environment (lighting, camera angles, customer density) differed significantly from standard YOLO training data, so the baseline model had insufficient recognition accuracy. Fully on-premise analysis without cloud dependency was required.
challenge2.alternatives: Cloud Vision APIs (AWS Rekognition, Google Vision) were rejected because streaming live CCTV footage to the cloud in real-time incurs bandwidth costs and latency, making stable real-time analysis infeasible on Malaysian store network conditions. Using a pre-trained model without adaptation was rejected because recognition accuracy was too low in the store-specific environment (high camera angles, varied lighting conditions) to be usable in practice.
challenge2.decision: I fine-tuned the YOLO model on store-specific CCTV data and deployed a bare-metal Linux server on-site at the store. This created a fully self-contained pipeline from video capture through analysis to result delivery, with no cloud dependency.
challenge2.implementation: The YOLO model was additionally trained on footage collected from the store's CCTV cameras to achieve store-specific recognition accuracy. On the Linux server, I implemented a sequential pipeline: video capture → YOLO inference → customer ID assignment → tracking → behavioral metric extraction. Extracted data was delivered in real-time to the VanillaJS dashboard via WebSocket.
challenge2.outcome: Delivered a fully on-premise analysis architecture with no cloud dependency, completing a stable real-time video capture and analysis system tailored to the store environment. A 3-person team successfully built and operated the CCTV-based customer behavior analysis system.

scholarlyChain.title: Scholarly Chain
scholarlyChain.subtitle: Hyperledger Fabric Blockchain-based Student Fee Management System

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.background: Scholarly Chain is a Hyperledger Fabric blockchain-based student fee transparency management system developed as a capstone design project. The goal was to record student fee revenue and expenditure on the blockchain to ensure transparency, allowing students to check fee usage in real-time. I was 100% responsible for the frontend built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, implementing role-based push notifications using Firebase Cloud Messaging and JWT-based authentication. The backend was integrated with a Hyperledger Fabric blockchain network, and the frontend called backend APIs to provide blockchain data to users.
overview.contribution: In a 4-member team, I was solely responsible for all frontend development, creating over 15 pages and 30+ reusable components. I implemented a JWT automatic token refresh middleware to prevent user session disconnection, and designed a role-based UI system providing different dashboards and features for students, committee members, and administrators. Using the shadcn/ui component library, I built a consistent design system and integrated Firebase Cloud Messaging to implement a push notification system that selectively sends notifications (payment confirmation, expenditure approval, etc.) based on roles. I utilized Next.js API Routes as a proxy to relay backend API calls and deployed on Vercel to configure the actual service environment.

retrospective.title: Retrospective
retrospective.growth: Leading a large-scale frontend project using Next.js and shadcn/ui from start to finish greatly strengthened my practical capabilities with modern frontend development stacks. Implementing JWT authentication middleware and role-based access control gave me deep understanding of web application security and permission management, and building a push notification system through Firebase Cloud Messaging built real-time communication technology experience. Particularly as the sole frontend developer in a 4-member team creating over 15 pages and 30+ reusable components, the experience of independently designing and implementing a large-scale project greatly helped develop capabilities. Design system building experience using shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS taught me how to maintain component reusability and consistency, and designing frontend-backend communication architecture through API Route proxy patterns also improved capabilities.
retrospective.improvement: Not writing test code early in the project led to frequent regression bugs as features were added. Especially for complex logic like authentication or role-based UI where unit tests are essential, skipping them due to schedule pressure was regrettable. Next time I want to secure test coverage at least for core business logic to improve stability. Also, handling state management only with Context API caused prop drilling issues as component depth increased. Had I introduced a lightweight state management library like Zustand or Jotai, code would have been more concise and maintainable. Not sufficiently considering reusability during initial component design meant having to create similar components multiple times later. In the next project, I want to systematically design component structure from the design stage and consider testing and state management from the beginning to build a more robust system.

challenge1.title: JWT Auto-Renewal Middleware and Auth Architecture Design
challenge1.context: In the blockchain-integrated student fee management system, 3 roles (student/committee/admin) each required different dashboards and permissions. Pages for reviewing fee history and verifying blockchain transactions required long sessions, but JWT expiration causing session disconnection would severely degrade user experience.
challenge1.alternatives: Session-based authentication (express-session) was rejected due to server state dependency making it incompatible with Vercel's serverless environment. NextAuth.js was rejected because its App Router support was unstable at the time and it was difficult to flexibly implement the custom authentication flow (API Routes proxy) needed for the blockchain backend.
challenge1.decision: I implemented JWT with a custom middleware approach. Next.js middleware automatically renews tokens before expiration to prevent session disconnection, API Routes proxy backend authentication requests, and route access is controlled based on the role claim in the JWT token.
challenge1.implementation: Next.js middleware checks JWT expiry on every request and auto-refreshes via refresh token when within threshold. API Routes proxy requests to the Hyperledger Fabric backend while passing the token. Role-based route guards (student/committee/admin) are enforced at the middleware level, redirecting on unauthorized access attempts.
challenge1.outcome: Implemented 15+ pages and 30+ reusable components, deploying successfully on Vercel. As the sole frontend developer in a 4-person team, built a 3-role authentication system with JWT auto-renewal that eliminates session disconnection.

challenge2.title: Hyperledger Fabric Blockchain Integration Proxy Design
challenge2.context: All transactions needed to be recorded on the Hyperledger Fabric blockchain for transparent student fee management. However, direct frontend access to blockchain nodes would expose complex SDK logic — including certificate management and network configuration — to the client side, creating security vulnerabilities.
challenge2.alternatives: Directly calling the Hyperledger SDK from the frontend was rejected because certificates and network configuration would be exposed to the client, posing security risks and significantly increasing bundle size. Adding a GraphQL layer was rejected because the blockchain query patterns were simple (recording/retrieving transactions), making a GraphQL schema unnecessarily over-engineered.
challenge2.decision: I used Next.js API Routes as a proxy layer. The frontend only calls internal API Routes, which relay requests to the blockchain backend server, encapsulating SDK complexity on the server side and keeping frontend code simple.
challenge2.implementation: API Routes validate JWT before forwarding requests to the backend blockchain server. FCM push notifications were integrated to send real-time role-specific alerts on fee deposits and expenditures. Blockchain transaction history was visualized in table and card formats using shadcn/ui components, providing a transparency dashboard accessible to all students.
challenge2.outcome: All blockchain-integrated UI was implemented using the API Routes proxy pattern across 30+ reusable components, completely eliminating blockchain SDK dependencies from the frontend code. As the sole frontend developer in a 4-person team, built 15+ pages and deployed successfully on Vercel.

dinoGo.title: Dino Go
dinoGo.subtitle: Sui Blockchain Location-based NFT Collection Game

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.background: Dino Go is a Sui blockchain-based location-based NFT collection game project conducted during a 3-day hackathon. It's a game where users collect virtual dinosaur NFTs by moving to actual locations and can trade collected NFTs on a marketplace. Google Maps API and Three.js were combined to implement a 3D map interface, NFT metadata is stored on Walrus decentralized storage, and data is protected with Seal threshold encryption. The frontend consists of Next.js, TypeScript, Three.js, and Tailwind CSS, while the backend comprises 4 Move smart contract modules and a Sui SDK-based Web3 communication layer.
overview.contribution: In a 4-member team, I was responsible for the entire frontend, implementing over 10 pages including NFT Studio (minting interface), Marketplace UI, and 3D map interface. I integrated Google Maps API with Three.js to overlay 3D dinosaur characters and interactive elements on the map, implementing coordinate transformation logic so 3D objects render at accurate positions even when users drag or zoom the map. In NFT Studio, I provided a UI where users can mint NFTs and upload metadata to Walrus, while Marketplace implemented NFT list viewing, search, filtering, and trading features. I developed 3 custom Web3 client libraries integrating Sui SDK, Walrus, Seal, and Kiosk SDK to abstract communication with blockchain and decentralized storage on the frontend.

retrospective.title: Retrospective
retrospective.growth: Developing the entire frontend under extreme time constraints of a 3-day hackathon made me experience the importance of quick decision-making and priority setting. Through 3D graphics implementation using Three.js and Google Maps API integration experience, I could handle a unique tech stack combining WebGL rendering with map services, and gained blockchain frontend development capabilities by utilizing Web3 tech stacks (Sui SDK, Move, Walrus, Seal) in practice. Particularly while designing and implementing custom Web3 client libraries, I developed architecture design capabilities to create frontend developer-friendly interfaces by abstracting complex external SDKs. Through solving synchronization problems between two rendering systems during Google Maps and Three.js integration, I gained low-level rendering optimization and performance tuning experience. Completing features and demoing within hackathon's fast development pace was thanks to clear priority setting and smooth team collaboration.
retrospective.improvement: Limited 3-day time forced compromising code quality. No test code was written at all, and error handling was implemented minimally leaving high bug possibility in edge cases. If developing into a production environment, thorough refactoring and securing test coverage are essential. Mobile optimization was also insufficient. Three.js rendering consumed much battery on mobile causing heating issues, but fundamental optimization wasn't done due to time shortage. Future work needs optimization like reducing WebGL rendering frequency or scaling back 3D effects on mobile. Much room for Three.js performance optimization remains. Applying advanced optimization techniques like model compression, texture atlases, and instancing could further improve performance. Hackathon experience made me clearly understand the difference between 'quickly making prototypes' and 'writing stable production code,' and in future projects I want to invest more time in initial design to build solid foundations.

challenge1.title: Google Maps + Three.js Coordinate Synchronization System
challenge1.context: In the Sui blockchain location-based NFT collection game, 3D dinosaur models needed to be overlaid on Google Maps. When users drag or zoom the map, 3D objects must follow their exact geographic positions — but Google Maps' latitude/longitude coordinate system and Three.js's 3D world coordinate system are entirely different, making real-time synchronization the core technical challenge.
challenge1.alternatives: Using 2D images as map markers was rejected because 3D interactions (rotation, animation) would be impossible, eliminating the core game experience. Implementing a custom map renderer with Three.js alone was rejected as impractical within the 3-day hackathon timeline — tile rendering, zoom levels, and satellite imagery processing would take far too long to build from scratch.
challenge1.decision: I separated Google Maps and Three.js into distinct layers. Google Maps handles the map rendering, and Three.js overlays a transparent Canvas on top. I implemented latitude/longitude ↔ pixel ↔ 3D world coordinate transformation logic directly to synchronize real-time with drag and zoom events.
challenge1.implementation: Extended Google Maps' OverlayView API to mount the Three.js Scene as an overlay. Whenever map events (drag, zoom_changed) fire, a coordinate transformation function converts lat/lng → pixel → Three.js world coordinates and updates positions of all 3D dinosaur objects. 3D model scale is also adjusted dynamically based on zoom level.
challenge1.outcome: Completed a coordinate synchronization system where 3D dinosaur objects render at accurate positions during map drag and zoom, across 10+ pages (NFT Studio, Marketplace, 3D Map, etc.) delivered in a 3-day hackathon. Led all frontend development as the sole frontend engineer in a 4-person team.

challenge2.title: Web3 Client Library Abstraction Layer
challenge2.context: Multiple services in the Sui blockchain ecosystem (Sui SDK, Walrus decentralized storage, Seal threshold encryption, Kiosk SDK) needed to be used on the frontend, but each SDK had different interfaces and inconsistent wallet connection and transaction signing patterns, rapidly increasing code complexity. Handling each SDK individually during a 3-day hackathon would have severely slowed development speed.
challenge2.alternatives: Calling each SDK directly from components was rejected because SDK updates would require modifying every usage site, and distributed wallet connection state management increases bug potential. Using existing Web3 integration libraries (e.g., wagmi) was rejected due to insufficient Sui chain support and no coverage for ecosystem-specific SDKs like Walrus and Seal.
challenge2.decision: I implemented 3 custom Web3 client libraries from scratch. Each abstracts one SDK — Sui SDK, Walrus, and Seal/Kiosk — and exposes a unified interface so that wallet connection, transaction signing, and storage uploads follow a consistent calling pattern across the codebase.
challenge2.implementation: Each library exposes shared methods such as connect(), signAndExecute(), and upload() through a unified interface. The Walrus library handles decentralized NFT image storage, the Seal library protects NFT metadata with threshold encryption, and the Kiosk SDK wrapper encapsulates NFT marketplace transaction logic.
challenge2.outcome: Abstracted Sui SDK, Walrus, and Seal/Kiosk integrations through 3 custom client libraries, enabling consistent Web3 interface calls from 10+ pages. Delivered NFT minting, marketplace trading, and decentralized storage all within the 3-day hackathon timeline.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.background: Ministry of Truth is a project conducted over one week during the Moltiverse Hackathon's Agent+Token Track—an AI art tournament platform where AI agents participate autonomously. An MC (host) agent runs the tournament, AI artists submit artwork matching given topics, two AI judges score submissions, and spectators (users) bet on winners on the Monad blockchain. We launched the $MOT token directly on nad.fun to establish the project's token economy. The tournament follows a bracket structure (quarterfinals→semifinals→finals), with all state transitions performed autonomously by agents. The backend uses NestJS + TypeORM + Supabase PostgreSQL, frontend uses Next.js, and agents run on the OpenClaw framework deployed on AWS EC2.
overview.contribution: As one of two developers in a 4-member team, I handled full-stack development. This included designing and implementing the NestJS backend API (tournament state machine, betting system, judging system), building 5 Next.js frontend pages (Home, Chamber, Betting, Leaderboard, Admin), developing the Solidity smart contract (MOTBetting.sol) and deploying it to Monad mainnet, launching the $MOT token directly on nad.fun, and designing behavior rules for 3 OpenClaw agents (MC, Judge A, Judge B) along with their EC2 deployment and operations.

retrospective.title: Retrospective
retrospective.growth: Building an on-chain tournament platform operated by autonomous AI agents from scratch during a one-week hackathon significantly developed my full-stack architecture design capabilities spanning multiple domains. Designing AI agent behavior rules with the OpenClaw framework and enabling autonomous operation was a completely different paradigm from conventional web development, teaching me the perspective of designing 'systems where agents judge and act on their own.' Deploying smart contracts on Monad, a new blockchain ecosystem, and integrating with nad.fun tokens developed my ability to adapt quickly in environments lacking documentation. Integrating NestJS backend, Next.js frontend, Solidity smart contracts, and OpenClaw agents into a single system improved my interface design and data flow management capabilities across technology stacks.
retrospective.improvement: Limited one-week time resulted in insufficient test code and inadequate edge case handling for agent behavior. The recovery logic for unexpected API responses was incomplete, leading to situations requiring manual intervention during the hackathon. Additionally, insufficient time invested in frontend UI/UX left the design polish lacking. In future similar projects, I want to design agent error recovery scenarios more thoroughly and write integration tests for both frontend and agent systems to improve stability.

challenge1.title: LLM Cost-Optimized Agent Design
challenge1.context: In the Moltiverse hackathon, 3 agent types — MC (host), Judge A (technical aesthetics), Judge B (thematic consistency) — needed to run autonomously 24/7. With each agent calling LLMs on every round, API costs risked escalating rapidly over the one-week hackathon. Vision models (used for image critique) are significantly more expensive than text models, making cost control a critical engineering challenge.
challenge1.alternatives: Using a single OpenAI GPT-4 model was rejected because, while it handles both vision and text, the cost of 24/7 autonomous operation was projected to exceed the hackathon budget. Self-hosting open-source LLMs was rejected because the GPU server cost and setup time for hosting vision models would be unrealistic within a one-week hackathon timeline.
challenge1.decision: I applied a Kimi (free credits) → Gemini Flash fallback strategy for the MC Agent using the OpenClaw framework. When free credits are exhausted, the system automatically switches to a lower-cost model to minimize expenses. For Judge A and Judge B, Kimi/Gemini Flash vision models are used with image critique requests capped at 1 per round.
challenge1.implementation: Each agent was configured with an LLM call priority chain (Kimi primary → Gemini Flash fallback). The system includes automatic fallback on API call failure and retry logic on response errors. The NestJS REST API tracks per-agent call counts for cost monitoring.
challenge1.outcome: Using the Kimi free credits + Gemini Flash fallback strategy, operated all 3 agents autonomously 24/7 for a full week while minimizing LLM API costs. Built a fully autonomous agent system running the 8-team → 4-team → finals tournament within the hackathon timeline.

challenge2.title: 6-Phase Autonomous Round State Machine
challenge2.context: The core of ArtWar is that the entire competition runs autonomously through agents. A 6-phase flow — topic announcement → submission → betting → judging → results → next round preview — needed to progress automatically based on timers and external events (agent submissions, user bets). A single phase failure could halt the entire round.
challenge2.alternatives: Simple cron-based scheduling was rejected because phase transition conditions depend not only on timers but also on participant actions (submission deadline, betting deadline), making pure timer-based scheduling insufficient. Event queues (RabbitMQ, Redis Streams) were rejected as over-engineered for a one-week hackathon and incompatible with the single AWS EC2 instance constraint.
challenge2.decision: I implemented a state machine pattern directly within NestJS. SQLite/JSON manages the world state (current round, phase, participants, betting status), and phase transitions trigger conditionally when each phase's completion criteria are met. Agent processes and the API server run together on a single AWS EC2 instance.
challenge2.implementation: Round state is defined as 6 phase enums, automatically advancing to the next phase when completion criteria (timer expiry OR participant action complete) are satisfied. The MC Agent handles topic generation (LLM call) → Moltbook posting → timer setup. Judge A/B handle judging (vision model call) → score calculation → result posting. Betting pool settlement and smart contract resolveRound calls execute automatically during the results phase.
challenge2.outcome: The 6-phase round flow ran completely autonomously through agents, running the 8-team → 4-team → finals tournament without human intervention. The scoring system combines Judge A (technique 40% + color 30% + interpretation 20% + emotion 10%) and Judge B (technique 10% + color 20% + interpretation 30% + emotion 40%) at equal final weight.

challenge3.title: Solidity Smart Contract Betting System
challenge3.context: The core of ArtWar's token economy is agents and users betting MON tokens to predict round winners. Prize distribution based on betting outcomes needed to be transparent and automated, with no possibility of manipulation. The project required launching the $MOT token on nad.fun and operating a betting contract on Monad mainnet.
challenge3.alternatives: Server-side betting (recorded in DB) was rejected due to trust issues — operators could manipulate results — and it conflicted with the decentralized philosophy of the agent economy. Forking an existing betting protocol (e.g., Polymarket) was rejected because Monad chain is unsupported and those protocols don't match ArtWar's specific round lifecycle (openRound→placeBet→closeBetting→resolveRound→claimWinnings).
challenge3.decision: I implemented ArtWarBetting.sol from scratch in Solidity 0.8.20. The functions openRound, placeBet, closeBetting, resolveRound, and claimWinnings manage the full round lifecycle on-chain, with a 5% fee structure for sustainable operations.
challenge3.implementation: openRound() creates a new round and opens betting, placeBet() records MON token bets (msg.value), closeBetting() closes the betting window, resolveRound() confirms the winner and enables settlement, and claimWinnings() distributes proportional payouts to winners (minus 5% fee). The agent API server automatically calls resolveRound after confirming round results.
challenge3.outcome: Deployed ArtWarBetting smart contract on Monad mainnet with 5 lifecycle functions and launched the $MOT token on nad.fun to establish the agent economy. Delivered a fully autonomous betting system where the entire flow — betting → settlement → claim — is handled transparently on-chain, all within a one-week hackathon.
